# Recommendation
Choose `std::sort`. It is the overwhelmingly superior choice for sorting 10,000,000 double-precision values in C++. Relying on the standard library implementation guarantees robust performance because it typically employs IntroSort, a hybrid algorithm that combines QuickSort, HeapSort, and InsertionSort. This approach prevents the worst-case quadratic behavior of naive QuickSort while maintaining excellent average-case efficiency. Implementing a custom QuickSort introduces significant maintenance overhead and risks severe performance penalties due to suboptimal pivot selection or poor cache utilization.

# Supporting basis
The primary justification is that `std::sort` is highly optimized by compiler vendors and standard library authors, leveraging architecture-specific intrinsics and sophisticated tuning. A custom QuickSort often fails to handle edge cases efficiently and may exhibit unstable performance on specific data distributions, even uniform ones, due to inadequate partitioning strategies. Furthermore, `std::sort` automatically switches to InsertionSort for small subarrays, reducing function call overhead. For 10^7 elements, the constant factors and cache-aware optimizations in the standard library provide a decisive speed advantage. Writing your own sorting algorithm rarely beats highly tuned library code unless you possess deep expertise in low-level optimization, which is rarely justified for general-purpose applications.<|im_end|>
